notes.meaning: God speaks to the people of Judah, most likely the exiles in Babylon. They carry the proud family names Jacob and Israel. They swear by the LORD, call themselves citizens of the holy city Jerusalem, and say they lean on God. But it is only an outward show, because their hearts are not true or right. The title "LORD of Hosts" reminds them that this God is strong enough to hold them to account.

God reminds them that he told them the "former things" long before they happened. These were events in Israel's story, such as Egypt, the Exodus and even the coming captivity, which Moses had warned about. Then God suddenly made them happen. The timing was so unexpected that no human cleverness could have guessed it.

God knew his people were stubborn. A neck of iron will not bow to him. A forehead of bronze is shameless and cannot blush at sin. So God announced things ahead of time, and they could not give the credit to their idols. This was patience, not just a scolding: God was piling up proof to win them back.

They had heard the prophecies, and now they could see them come true. Will they not admit it and tell others, as God's witnesses? Now God announces "new things" that were hidden. The first of these is rescue from Babylon through King Cyrus. Many also see here a look ahead to Christ and the good news of the gospel.

"Created now" means these things are being brought to light for the first time, almost like a new creation. God kept them hidden until now. That way the people could not boast, "I knew that already!" God guards against human pride that wants to take credit for his work.

For a long time their ears had been closed to God. He knew they would be unfaithful. They had been rebels "from birth," which many take to mean from the nation's birth at the Exodus out of Egypt. Matthew Henry also applies it to everyone: we are all born with a bent toward sin, and wrong actions follow. Even so, God does not treat us as we deserve.

God holds back his anger, as if putting a muzzle on it, so that his people are not wiped out. He does this not because they deserve it, but for the sake of his own name. If he destroyed them, the nations would mock him. By sparing them, he will be praised for his mercy.

Silver is kept in the fire until every bit of waste is burned away. If God did that to his people, nothing would be left, because they were all waste. So he refined them only in part, and gently. The "furnace of affliction" was the hard captivity in Babylon, which God used to test them and make them his own.

God will rescue them for his own sake. If he left them in Babylon, enemies would sneer at his name and give the credit to their idols. He will not let his glory go to another. It is a comfort that God ties his people's rescue to his own honor.

After hard words, God still calls them "Israel, whom I have called," the way a father still owns a son he has rebuked. "I am He" means he never changes. He is the first, before everything, and the last, outlasting everything. So he will be to them what he has always been.
God's own hand laid the earth's foundation and spread out the sky. When he calls them, they stand ready to obey. The God who made and rules everything can surely rescue his people.

God calls everyone together and asks which idol ever foretold this. The one the LORD has chosen and "loves" is Cyrus, the Persian king, who will carry out God's will against Babylon. "Loved" here means chosen and favored for a task. It is not the saving love God has for his children.
God says it twice: it is he who has spoken. He called Cyrus and led him step by step, and so Cyrus will succeed. His victories are really God's work, so neither idols nor luck can take the credit.

God invites them to come near and listen. He has always spoken openly, not in riddles, and he was there guiding events as they happened. Then a voice says, "The Lord GOD has sent me, with His Spirit." Many older writers take this as the prophet, sent by God and his Spirit, who is also a picture of Christ. Jesus was sent too, and he had the Spirit without limit.

differ.view: Some believe the Messiah himself is speaking here, leading into Isaiah 49, where God's Servant speaks.

notes.meaning: God calls himself their Redeemer, the one who buys back and sets free his people, and the Holy One of Israel. He teaches them what is truly good for them and leads them in the right way. His teaching, including the lessons of hard times, is for their benefit. If they do not benefit, the fault is theirs, not his.

"If only you had listened!" is God's tender sigh, like a father grieving for his children. It is much like Jesus weeping over Jerusalem. Obedience would have brought blessing that kept flowing like a river, and goodness as steady as the waves. They would have had countless children, as God promised Abraham. Instead their numbers shrank and they were cut off from their land.

Now comes the call to go free: leave Babylon, and go with shouts of joy! Many exiles were tempted to stay put, but God tells them to go and to tell the whole world that he has rescued his servant Jacob. Many also see here a picture of the gospel being announced to the ends of the earth.

This looks back to the Exodus, when God gave water from the rock in the desert. The prophet uses that picture to promise that God will care for them on the road home from Babylon too. Matthew Henry also sees in it the grace that flows to us from Christ, for "that Rock was Christ."

The chapter ends with a warning. These promises of peace do not belong to the wicked, who reject God and will not change. They have no peace with God and no peace in their own hearts. The same line closes another section of Isaiah, at 57:21.
